Screen Size

The resolution the game runs at. Lower is faster but less sharp; higher is sharper but heavier. The picture is then scaled to fit your screen, and the Scaling mode in the game side menu (for example SGSR HQ) decides how.

New containers start at a size that matches your screen shape — 1280x720 on 16:9 and wider screens, 1280x800 on 16:10 and 1280x960 on 4:3 — so the picture can fill the screen.

Examples: a heavy game stutters → try 960x544 or 854x480 with SGSR HQ. A light game on a 1080p screen → 1920x1080 for full sharpness. A 4:3 handheld → 1280x960.

Faster BCn layer

Uses Fcharan\'s build of leegao\'s BCn texture layer (from WinlatorMali 1.2, 2026-10-22) instead of the bundled one. Its author says it loads textures faster with the same memory use.

Try it on a Mali GPU when textures take long to appear or a game stutters while loading. If textures break or the game crashes, turn it off again. The ETC2 / ASTC transcode choices are not used by this build. Mali GPUs only; nothing changes on other GPUs.

Credit: Fcharan (GunaCharanTeja, WinlatorMali) and leegao (bcn_layer, MIT).

Dynamic recompiler — the heart of Box64. It translates the game x86 code into ARM code once, then reuses the translation.

0 : Interpret every instruction one at a time. Correct, but many times slower and not realistically playable. Debugging only.
1 : Translate and cache. This is what makes games run at usable speed. (default)

When to change: Never turn this off for playing. It exists for diagnosing a suspected translation bug: if a game misbehaves on 1 but is correct on 0, the fault is in the recompiler rather than the game.

Secondary entry points for CALL/RET. Lets Box64 jump into the middle of a block it already translated instead of building a near-identical copy.

0 : One entry point per block. More duplicate blocks, more memory.
1 : Add secondary entry points. Fewer duplicates, slightly faster. (default)
2 : More aggressive still.

Only has an effect when DYNAREC_CALLRET is on.

When to change: Leave it at the default. Worth lowering only if you are already turning CALLRET off for a packed or DRM-protected executable, since the two work together.

How much bookkeeping Box64 keeps for each translated block. That bookkeeping is what lets it notice when code or memory changes and re-translate correctly.

0 : Keep everything. Safest. (default)
1 : Trim some. Less memory.
2 : Trim aggressively. Least memory, most likely to misbehave.

When to change: raise it only if you are short on RAM — it trades correctness for memory. Set it back to 0 first if a game starts crashing after previously running fine on the same preset.

64-bit Windows programs can carry volatile metadata: the compiler marking exactly which memory accesses must not be reordered. Box64 can read it and enforce strict ordering only where the game genuinely needs it, instead of everywhere.

0 : Ignore it.
1 : Use it. Usually faster than blanket STRONGMEM while staying correct. (default)

Only applies to 64-bit Windows games built with the metadata present.

When to change: Leave it on — it costs nothing and simply has no effect on games built without the metadata. Turning it off is only useful to check whether it is masking a different ordering problem.

Whether translated blocks are kept on disk between runs so the next launch starts warm.

0 : Off. Translate fresh every launch. (default)
1 / 2 : Increasing levels of caching. Faster startup and fewer first-time stutters, at the cost of disk space.

Clear the container cache after a game update if you see odd behaviour.

When to change: Turn it on if a game takes a long time to warm up every session, or stutters in the same places on every launch. Clear the container cache after a game update, since a stale cache can produce odd behaviour.

AES-NI, the hardware encryption instructions. Games, DRM and anti-cheat use them heavily.

0 : Tell the game the CPU has no AES. Anything using it falls back to slow software encryption, or picks a different code path.
1 : Advertise AES and map it onto the ARM equivalents, so it runs at near-native speed. (default)

Turn it off only if a game misdetects the CPU and refuses to start.

When to change: Leave it on — it maps to real ARM instructions, so it is close to free. Turn it off only if a game misdetects the CPU and refuses to start.

Carry-less multiply — a specialised instruction used by encryption and checksum code, often alongside AES.

0 : Hide it. Callers fall back to slower software routines.
1 : Advertise it and map it to the ARM equivalent. (default)

When to change: Leave it on. It only matters for games doing heavy encryption or checksum work, where hiding it makes loading and verification noticeably slower.

SHA extensions — hardware SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashing, used for file verification, save integrity checks and DRM.

0 : Hide it. Hashing falls back to software and gets slower.
1 : Advertise it and map it to the ARM equivalent. (default)

When to change: Leave it on. Hiding it slows down any game that verifies its own files at startup, since every hash falls back to software.

SSE4.2 — string and text processing instructions plus hardware CRC32.

0 : Hide it. Some modern games check for SSE4.2 at startup and refuse to run without it.
1 : Advertise it. (default)

Leave this on unless a game specifically misbehaves with it.

When to change: Leave it on. Several modern games test for SSE4.2 during startup and exit immediately without it, usually with an unhelpful error or no message at all.

How denormals — extremely small floating-point numbers — are handled in SSE maths.

0 : Full IEEE behaviour with exception flags tracked. Correct, but slow whenever a game produces denormals. (default)
1 : Flush denormals straight to zero, which is what most game engines ask for anyway. Faster, and can very slightly change physics or audio results.

When to change: Set it to 1 for a speed gain in games with heavy physics or audio processing, which generate denormals constantly. Set it back to 0 if physics or sound behave subtly differently from how they should.

x87 is the old floating-point unit. It works in 80-bit extended precision, which ARM has no equivalent for, so Box64 has to emulate it.

0 : Emulate full 80-bit precision. Accurate but slow.
1 : Use ordinary 64-bit doubles instead. Much faster, and what the fast presets pick.

Older games doing precise maths — physics, simulation, flight models — can drift or behave oddly on 1.

When to change: Leave at 1 for modern games, which barely touch x87. Set it to 0 for older simulation-style games — flight sims, racing physics, strategy titles with large numbers — where accumulated precision loss shows up as drift over a long session.

Which CPU vendor Box64 reports to the game.

0 : Intel (default)
1 : AMD

Some games, DRM and anti-cheat take different code paths depending on the vendor, and a few refuse to run on one of them. Only worth changing if a specific title needs it.

When to change: Only change it for a specific title that needs it. Some games and anti-cheat take a different code path per vendor, and a few refuse to run on one of them outright.

Marks the process as a Unity game so Box64 applies Unity-specific workarounds, mostly around its Mono and IL2CPP runtimes and how they handle threads.

0 : Off (default)
1 : On

Worth trying if a Unity game crashes at startup or hangs on a loading screen.

When to change: Turn it on if a Unity game crashes at startup or hangs on a loading screen. It is a no-op for everything else, so it is safe to leave on for a container dedicated to Unity titles.

The largest number of guest instructions FEX will pack into a single translated block.

Bigger blocks run faster, because FEX can optimise across more of the game code at once and jumps between blocks cost time. They also take longer to compile and use more memory, so a very large value can cause hitching the first time new code runs.

5000 is the default and suits almost everything. Lower it only if you are chasing memory use or startup stutter.

When to change: Leave it at 5000. Lower it if you are chasing memory use, or if a game hitches badly the first time it reaches new code and you would rather have smaller, quicker compiles.

How hard FEX watches for self-modifying code — a program writing or rewriting its own instructions while running. FEX has to notice, or it keeps running a stale translation of code that has since changed.

none : No checking. Fastest, and what the Extreme presets use. Breaks anything that generates code at runtime: Java and .NET runtimes, some launchers, and most DRM.
mtrack : Track writes to memory pages holding translated code. The balanced default.
full : Check thoroughly. Slowest and safest — what the Denuvo preset uses.

If a game runs on Performance but not on an Extreme preset, this is the first thing to change back.

When to change: If a game runs on Performance but not on an Extreme preset, this is the first thing to change back. Set it to full for a Denuvo-protected title, which will not start otherwise.

How eagerly the dynamic L1 block cache grows.

The L1 cache holds recently used translated blocks. When it fills, FEX either grows it or starts discarding blocks it will likely need again. This number is how much pressure it takes before growing: lower grows sooner, spending memory to avoid re-translating.

Default 250. Only has any effect when DYNAMICL1CACHE is on.

When to change: Lower it if you see stutter in busy scenes and have memory to spare. Raise it on a memory-tight device. It does nothing at all unless DYNAMICL1CACHE is on.

How eagerly the dynamic L1 block cache shrinks back down.

After a busy stretch — a level load, a big area transition — the cache may be far larger than the game now needs. This number is how long it waits before handing memory back: higher holds memory longer, which avoids shrinking and regrowing repeatedly.

Default 50. Only has any effect when DYNAMICL1CACHE is on.

When to change: Raise it if you get a hitch shortly after a level load, which usually means the cache shrank and then had to grow straight back. Lower it to hand memory back sooner. It does nothing at all unless DYNAMICL1CACHE is on.
Stability — maximum correctness. Full CPU flag emulation, no fast maths, full 80-bit x87 precision and no block merging. The slowest option: reach for it when a game crashes on everything else.
Compatibility — the same conservative maths as Stability with a little more freedom for the translator. A good fallback when a game misbehaves on Intermediate.
Intermediate — the balanced default. Faster NaN handling and light block merging, while keeping safe CPU flags and full x87 precision. Start here.

Performance — noticeably faster: relaxed flags, fast rounding, 64-bit x87 and aggressive block merging.

Small risk of maths or precision glitches in games sensitive to rounding.
Performance (Mali) — Performance retuned for Mali GPUs: CPU flag emulation off but exact rounding kept, which suits Mali drivers better. No benefit on Adreno.

Extreme — Performance plus deeper instruction look-ahead, call/return optimisation and AVX disabled. Faster again.

Wider blast radius: a game sensitive to timing or maths is more likely to misbehave than on Performance.

Extreme-2 — the community 32-variable tuning. Everything Extreme does, pushed further: faster rounding, double the look-ahead, native CPU flags, and the AES, SSE4.2, SHA and PCLMULQDQ instruction sets exposed to the game.

Risk: it also weakens memory barriers, which can corrupt multi-threaded state. That shows up as random instability rather than a clean crash — drop back to Extreme if a game turns flaky.
Unity — Performance retuned for Unity games, with the stronger memory ordering most Unity titles need to stay stable.
Unity Mono Bleeding Edge — for newer Unity builds on the bleeding-edge Mono runtime. Disables the block merging that upsets its just-in-time compiler.
Denuvo — conservative settings for Denuvo-protected games, which detect and dislike aggressive translation. Slower by design; use it only for titles that need it.
Stability — every memory-ordering emulation enabled plus full x87 precision. The slowest and most correct option; use it when nothing else runs.
Compatibility — full memory-ordering emulation, same as Stability. Broad correctness at the cost of speed.
Intermediate — the balanced default. Keeps the main and half-barrier ordering, drops the heavier vector and memcpy ordering, and allows reduced x87 precision.

Performance — all memory-ordering emulation off. Clearly faster.

Risk: games that rely on strict store ordering can crash, hang or corrupt saves. If that happens, use Performance (TSO).

Performance (TSO) — Performance with the main store-ordering emulation switched back on, while the heavier vector, half-barrier and memcpy ordering stay off. The best general compromise, and the safest fast option.

Extreme-wn — from WinNative. Performance plus five JIT and cache knobs: self-modifying-code checks off, the L2 block cache off, and a dynamically sized L1 cache.

Risk: with code checks off, anything that writes its own code while running — Java or .NET runtimes, some launchers and DRM — can misbehave. Memory ordering is also off, so this is the most aggressive tier available.

Extreme (TSO)-wn — the same tuning as Extreme-wn but with store ordering kept on, so it suits far more games. This is the one to try first if you want more speed than Performance (TSO).

Risk: self-modifying-code checks are off, which can break Java or .NET runtimes, some launchers and DRM. Fall back to Extreme-gn if that bites.

Extreme-gn — from GameNative, and much gentler than the name suggests. Performance plus timer scaling and volatile-metadata hints only, leaving code checks and the block caches at their defaults.

The safer Extreme: try this when a game will not run on the two WinNative tiers.
Denuvo — for Denuvo-protected games. Memory ordering off for speed, but full self-modifying-code checking and a hidden hypervisor bit, both of which Denuvo needs to start.

WineD3D is a translation layer for DirectX 1-11 to OpenGL.

DXVK is a translation layer for Direct3D 9-11 to Vulkan.

VEGAS is a performance-tuned fork of DXVK with game-specific optimizations for Android/Adreno devices.

VKD3D is a translation layer for Direct3D 12 API to Vulkan.

CNC DDraw is an implementation of DirectDraw for better compatibility with classic games.

Anisotropic filtering

Keeps textures sharp when you see them at an angle — the road ahead of a car, floors, walls running into the distance. Without it they turn blurry a short way ahead.

Game default leaves it to the game. 2x to 16x forces it on; higher stays sharp further away. It costs little on most devices; if you lose FPS, try 4x or 8x.

Example: the track in a racing game looks smeared just ahead of the car → 16x.

DirectX 9–11 games only (DXVK / VEGAS). Applies the next time the game starts.

Texture sharpness

Makes the game use its more detailed textures. Most useful when the game runs below your screen resolution with an upscaler on, where textures otherwise look softer than the rest of the picture.

Game default changes nothing. Auto picks the right amount for the Scaling mode the game starts with (set in the game side menu: SGSR, SGSR HQ, FSR or NIS) — about -0.58 for 720p on a 1080p screen — and does nothing without one. Sharper / Sharpest use a fixed amount; a bigger number is sharper.

Example: a game at 720p with SGSR HQ on a 1080p screen → Auto.

Too sharp makes fine detail (gravel, fences, grass) shimmer while moving — step back if you see that. DirectX 9–11 games only. Applies the next time the game starts.

Wine version

The compatibility layer that runs the Windows game — it translates Windows into Android without a real Windows install. Proton is a gaming-tuned build of Wine. Newer builds fix more games; leave it on the default unless a game needs a specific one.

Sync

Windows games constantly tell their threads to wait for each other (“wait until this is loaded”, “signal when the frame is ready”). Wine has several ways to handle that; the faster ones mean less stutter and CPU overhead. This setting picks which one the game uses. Options the selected compatibility layer can\'t do are greyed out.

esync — the default. Wine handles most waits with Linux event files instead of asking its background server each time. Fast and well tested.

ntsync — copies how Windows itself does it, so it is the most accurate and also fast. Only on layers built with it. New: try it per game. If it can\'t start, the game falls back to esync automatically.

fsync — a faster method used on Linux PCs (Steam Deck), built on a Linux feature Android blocks for apps. Always greyed out here; it cannot work on Android.

wineserver — no shortcut at all: every wait goes through Wine\'s background server. Slowest and heaviest on the CPU, but the most compatible — use it when a game hangs, stutters or misbehaves on the others.

Game settings follow the container unless you pick something else for that game.

Sets at launch: esync → WINEESYNC=1 · ntsync → WINENTSYNC=1 + WINEESYNC=1 · wineserver → WINEESYNC=0. Any of these typed into Environment Variables is replaced by this setting.

OpenGL settings

Fast — sends an OpenGL game\'s frames straight to the screen through Vulkan (the route DXVK games take) instead of copying every frame back first. Several times faster, and it also speeds up DirectDraw and older Direct3D games through WineD3D. It works with any Wine layer: layers with Wine\'s EGL backend go through EGL, everything else (older Wine, and every x86-64 layer) through GLX. It needs a Turnip graphics driver; without one it is greyed and games use the old path. On by default; turn it off for a game that shows a black screen, crashes or draws wrongly.

Show FPS — Mesa\'s frames-per-second counter in the top-left corner of OpenGL games. DXVK games don\'t show it. Off by default.

Vsync off — lets OpenGL games run above the screen\'s refresh rate instead of waiting for each refresh. You may see tearing. Off by default.

None of these speed up game time: a very old game that ties its speed to the frame rate can run too fast — cap it with the FPS limiter.

Auto (game settings) — follows the container\'s setting; On or Off applies to that game only. Changes take effect the next time the game starts.

Sets at launch: Fast → the bundled OpenGL libraries with Zink, plus WINE_USE_EGL=1 on the EGL route or the X server\'s GLX on the GLX route (WINHUB_X11_EGL=0 turns it off, WINHUB_X11_EGL=1 forces EGL, WINHUB_X11_GLX=1 forces GLX) · Show FPS → GALLIUM_HUD=fps · Vsync off → vblank_mode=0. A GALLIUM_HUD or vblank_mode you typed into Environment Variables is kept.

Graphics driver (wrapper)

The Vulkan driver the container uses to talk to your GPU. Different wrappers suit different GPUs — Adreno (Snapdragon) has the best support; Mali phones may need a specific wrapper to handle compressed textures. Stick with the default unless you\'re troubleshooting.

Renderer

How the game\'s image is delivered to your screen. Vulkan is the default and best for most games.

Present Mode controls how finished frames are handed to your screen — a trade-off between tearing, input lag and battery.

FIFO (default): \'Vsync on.\' Every frame waits its turn and is shown on the next refresh — smooth, tear-free and the most power-efficient. Downside: it makes the game wait for the display, which can hold back frame generation.

Mailbox: \'Fast vsync.\' The screen always grabs the newest frame and never makes the game wait — tear-free like FIFO but lower lag. Best for frame generation, since its extra generated frames actually reach the screen. Costs a little more battery (it may render frames it discards).

Immediate: \'Vsync off.\' Frames appear the instant they\'re ready — lowest lag, but you may see tearing. Rarely worth it on a high-refresh screen.

Tip: WinHub automatically switches to Mailbox while frame generation is multiplying, then back to your setting when it\'s off.
LSFG Native and Win-FG Native switch this to FIFO while they\'re generating, then restore your choice — they send the real and made-up frames together and need FIFO to show them one per refresh.

Download speed

Download speed sets how many pieces of the game download at once. Higher = faster, up to the limit of your internet connection and Steam\'s servers — it doesn\'t cap your speed. Lower settings use fewer connections to stay gentle on your device and network. Downloads run one at a time; extra games wait in the queue.

Slow

Fewest pieces at once. Lightest on your device and bandwidth, slowest overall. Good for downloading in the background while you play or use your phone.

Medium

A moderate number at once — a balance between speed and staying light.

Fast (default)

Lots of pieces at once for strong speed on most connections. Recommended.

Blazing

The most pieces at once — fastest, uses the most bandwidth and device resources. Best for big games on a fast connection.

GMEM (tiled rendering)

How the GPU draws each frame. GMEM (tiled) rendering splits the screen into small tiles and draws them in ultra-fast on-chip memory — the efficient, mobile-native way.

Auto turns it on only for Adreno 710/720/722 (which need it to avoid glitches); Force On applies it to any GPU; Force Off never does. Leave on Auto unless a game misbehaves. Its opposite is \'sysmem\'.

sysmem

Forces the GPU to draw straight to main memory instead of the fast on-chip tile memory — the opposite of GMEM. It\'s the most compatible option (and the default), but uses more memory bandwidth. Use it if forcing GMEM makes a game glitch.

Sync Every Frame

Makes the GPU fully finish and show each frame before starting the next (synchronous presentation). Turn it ON to fix tearing, flicker, or glitchy on-screen frames; leave it OFF for best performance, since it can cost some fps by stopping the CPU and GPU from working ahead of each other.

forcecb / nocb (concurrent binning)

Binning is the step where the GPU sorts what belongs in each on-screen tile. \'forcecb\' forces it to run alongside rendering (can help performance); \'nocb\' turns it off (can fix glitches on some games). Expert options — only touch them if a specific game needs it.

deck_emu

Makes the GPU report itself to the game as a Steam Deck, which can unlock better graphics settings or code paths in some games. Only works on WinHub\'s own (Banners-Turnip) drivers — ignored on stock Turnip.

Disable KHR_present_wait

Some GPU drivers implement Vulkan\'s \'present wait\' feature — which lets a game wait until a frame has actually appeared on screen — incorrectly, causing stalls or hangs. Turn this ON to make the driver stop using it, as a compatibility fallback. Leave it OFF unless a game freezes or won\'t display.

One UI / HyperOS Fix

A compatibility workaround for some Samsung (One UI) and Xiaomi (HyperOS) phones, whose GPU drivers need an extra texture-compression hint to render correctly. Turn it ON only if games show corruption or crash on those devices; leave it OFF otherwise.

BCn Emulation Type

Chooses HOW compressed game textures (BCn / DXT) are unpacked on GPUs that can\'t read them natively — Mali and other non-Adreno chips. Compute uses a GPU compute-shader layer (usually faster); software uses the wrapper\'s built-in decoder. No effect on Adreno, which reads BCn textures natively. Switch options if textures look wrong or a game runs slowly.

BCn Emulation Cache

When a GPU has to emulate compressed (BCn) textures, this keeps the already-decoded textures in a cache so they don\'t have to be unpacked again — reducing stutter and CPU/GPU work, at the cost of a little extra memory. No effect on Adreno (native BCn).

Transcode to ASTC

Instead of fully decompressing emulated BCn textures, this repacks them into ASTC — a compressed texture format that Mali and other mobile GPUs support in hardware. Can save memory and improve performance on those GPUs. Only honored by BCn-capable drivers; no effect on Adreno (native BCn).

Vulkan Version

The Vulkan version the graphics driver reports to the DirectX translator (DXVK / VKD3D). A higher number can unlock newer features some games ask for. It\'s automatically capped to what your driver actually supports, so picking a version above your driver\'s does nothing. Leave it at the default unless a game specifically needs a higher Vulkan level.

Graphics Driver Version

Which build of the GPU driver (Turnip / the Vulkan wrapper) to use for this game. Newer builds often fix bugs or add speed, but a specific game can run better on an older one. If a game glitches or won\'t start, try a different version here. Manage and import more drivers with the cloud button.

Show incompatible drivers

Also lists driver versions that WinHub thinks won\'t work with your phone\'s GPU. They\'re hidden by default to keep you from picking one that fails. Turn this on only if you want to experiment — an incompatible driver may crash or show a black screen.

GPU Name (spoofing)

Makes games see a different graphics card than your real one. Some games unlock better graphics options, or simply run, when they recognise a specific GPU. Leave it on \'Device\' to report your real GPU; pick a name to spoof it. Ignored when the DX wrapper is set to WineD3D.

Max Device Memory

Caps how much video memory (VRAM) the driver tells games it has. \'Default\' lets the driver report its own amount. Setting a specific limit can stop a game from trying to use more memory than your phone has — a fix for out-of-memory crashes or stutter in a few titles. Leave on Default unless a game misbehaves.

Present Modes

How finished frames are handed to the screen.

mailbox — low latency, always shows the newest frame (triple-buffered); the smooth default.
fifo — classic V-Sync: frames wait for the display, no tearing but can feel less responsive.
immediate — sends frames the instant they\'re ready: lowest latency but can tear.

Leave on mailbox unless you\'re chasing lower latency or fixing tearing.

Memory Resource Type

How the driver shares image memory between the game and the display. auto lets it choose the best method for your device and is right for almost everyone. The other options (dmabuf / AHB / opaque) are fallbacks — only switch if a game shows corrupted graphics or won\'t display on your specific phone.

BCn Emulation

Whether to emulate the compressed (BCn / DXT) textures that PC games use, for GPUs that can\'t read them natively — Mali and other non-Adreno chips. auto turns it on only where it\'s needed; full forces it; partial does a subset; none disables it. Has no effect on Adreno, which reads BCn textures in hardware. Leave on auto unless textures look wrong.

Available Extensions

Opens the list of optional Vulkan features (extensions) the driver offers, and lets you blacklist individual ones. This is an expert tool — turning an extension off can work around a driver bug that makes a specific game crash or render wrong. Leave everything enabled unless you\'re following a known fix.

Colors (BGRA / RGBA)

The order of the red and blue colour channels in the game\'s image. BGRA (the default) is correct for almost every game. Switch to RGBA only if a game\'s colours look swapped — blue where red should be. RGBA routes through the compositor, so it can\'t be combined with Native rendering.

Native Renderer

Sends the game\'s image straight to the screen instead of through WinHub\'s compositor. This lowers latency and can improve performance, but disables features that need the compositor — colour swapping (RGBA) and the present-mode control. Turn it off if a game shows the wrong colours or won\'t display correctly.

Renderer Driver

Which Vulkan driver the on-screen compositor runs on — the layer that takes your game\'s finished frame and puts it on screen. This is not where your game renders; that\'s the top-level Graphics Driver.

System (default) uses Android\'s own Vulkan driver — the safe, always-compatible choice. Picking an installed Turnip points the compositor at that build instead. It mostly affects present/compatibility behaviour, not your game\'s FPS (the compositor isn\'t where rendering happens).

Leave it on System unless you know you need otherwise: a Turnip compositor can black-screen on builds whose window-system support doesn\'t match your device.

Scaling mode

How the game picture is stretched to fill your screen. The upscalers matter most when a game runs below your screen resolution (for example 1280x720 on a 1080p screen), which is the usual way to get more FPS.

None / Linear / Nearest — plain stretching. Linear is smooth; Nearest keeps hard pixel edges.
SGSR — Snapdragon upscaler. Rebuilds edges so a lower resolution looks sharper. Very light.
SGSR HQ — SGSR with cleaner diagonal and curved edges, for about the same cost.
FSR / FSR (Fit) — AMD upscaler, a little heavier. FSR fills the whole screen (may stretch); FSR (Fit) keeps the shape and adds black bars.
NIS — NVIDIA upscaler, similar to FSR.
Sharpen — no upscaling, only sharpens. Works at any resolution.

Examples: a heavy game at 720p on a 1080p screen → SGSR HQ. A pixel-art or retro game → Nearest. A game already at your screen resolution → None, or Sharpen for extra crispness.

Sharpness sets how strong the sharpening is. Your choice is remembered for this game.

FPS Limiter

Loads the frame-rate limiter for this game. Turning it on just enables the feature — you set the actual cap (10–200 fps) live from the in-game FPS menu. Capping fps can cut heat and battery use, and smooth out an unstable frame rate. (While LSFG Native or Win-FG Native is running, the limiter is switched on automatically — frame generation needs a steady cap — so you only need this on its own for a cap without frame generation.)

Frame Generation

Adds made-up frames between the ones your game draws, so motion looks smoother. It can\'t make the game respond faster, and it adds a little input delay. Two engines:

Win-FG Native — built in, nothing to buy or import. Always 2×.
LSFG Native — Lossless Scaling\'s frame generation. Needs your own Lossless.dll, imported at the bottom of Settings. 2×, 3× or 4×.

Both need the Vulkan renderer. LSFG Native also needs a Renderer Driver with Vulkan 1.3 — on older Adreno GPUs, pick a Turnip driver there. If something is missing, the game\'s side menu says what and how to fix it.

Getting it right: in the game\'s side menu, set Max FPS to a number the game can always hold, then pick a multiplier so Max FPS × multiplier fits your screen\'s refresh rate (for example 48 × 3 = 144 Hz). Going over causes stutter and lag; the side menu warns you and offers a fix. Auto (match FPS) turns on while frame generation runs, fitting the screen to your numbers — turn it off there if you prefer.

Frame generation starts Off each launch; turn it on from the side menu. It\'s still new: if a game looks worse with it, leave it off for that game.

Audio Driver

How the game\'s sound reaches Android. PulseAudio is the default — a capable sound server that works for most games and voice features. ALSA is a lighter, low-overhead alternative. DirectAudio (Experimental) sends sound straight to Android with no server in between (lowest latency), but it\'s new — see its warning. Switch drivers if a game has no sound or crackles.

DirectAudio is experimental

It sends the game\'s sound straight to Android\'s audio system with no PulseAudio or ALSA server in between — the lowest-latency path, and it mixes all the game\'s sounds itself.

Because it\'s new, some games may have audio quirks — occasional skips, or a preset that doesn\'t stick. The Auto preset is the smoothest.

If you hit audio problems, switch back to PulseAudio or ALSA.

FEXCore Preset

FEXCore runs x86 games on your ARM phone. This preset trades accuracy for speed by tuning how faithfully it emulates the PC\'s memory ordering (TSO). Stability / Compatibility keep it fully accurate (safest, a little slower); Performance relaxes it for more fps (can break some games); the in-between and Denuvo presets are middle grounds for specific titles. Start on the default and move toward Performance only if a game runs but is slow.

FEXCore Version

Which build of the FEXCore x86-to-ARM translator to use for this game. Newer builds usually run more games and run them faster, but a specific title can prefer an older one. If a game crashes or won\'t start under FEXCore, try a different version. Import more with the download button.

Startup Selection

How many Windows background services Wine starts before your game. Normal loads them all (most compatible); Essential loads only the important ones; Aggressive stops extras to save memory and start faster. Custom lets you pick services one by one. If a game fails to launch, move back toward Normal.

Gyro Mode

How tilting the phone moves the aim. Rate — tilt SPEED aims, and it recentres when you hold still (like a mouse). Tilt to Aim — the ANGLE you hold aims, so a held tilt keeps aiming. Rate suits most shooters; Tilt to Aim suits fine, held adjustments. (Tilt to Aim can\'t drive the Mouse target.)

Gyro Activator

Which controller button switches gyro aiming on, so the phone isn\'t always steering. Pick a button you can hold while aiming (for example L2), or choose Always On to leave gyro active the whole time.

Gyro Activation Mode

How the activator button behaves. Hold — gyro aims only while you hold the button. Toggle — one press turns gyro on, another turns it off. Hold suits quick aim bursts; Toggle suits leaving it on hands-free.

Gyro Sensitivity

How far the aim moves for a given tilt. Higher values turn faster from a small movement; lower values give steadier, finer aim. Tune it to taste — start in the middle and adjust until aiming feels natural.

Gyro Target

What the phone\'s tilt actually controls. Right stick (the usual choice) aims like the right analog stick; Left stick moves like the left stick; Mouse drives the pointer for mouse-aim games. The Mouse target always uses Rate mode.

Handling of flags on CALL/RET opcodes

0 : Treats CALL/RET as if it never needed flags (faster, unstable)
1 : Most RET will need flags, most CALLS will not
2 : All CALL/RET will need flags (slower)

When to change: Lower it for speed in call-heavy games. Raise it to 2 if a game crashes shortly after launch or behaves erratically — missing flags around calls corrupt the decisions a program makes right after returning from a function.

NaN handling. x86 produces a negative NaN in some floating-point cases where ARM produces a positive one, and matching x86 exactly costs extra instructions on every such operation.

0 : Reproduce the x86 NaN sign exactly. Slower, bit-accurate.
1 : Let the ARM chip produce its natural NaN. Faster. (default)

When to change: leave on 1. Drop to 0 if a game shows stretched or invisible models, geometry shooting off to infinity, or physics exploding — classic signs of a NaN sign difference propagating through maths.

Rounding mode. x86 lets a program pick a rounding mode and expects it honoured on every floating-point operation; reproducing that on ARM costs work each time.

0 : Emulate x86 rounding precisely, all modes. Slowest and most accurate.
1 : Fast rounding covering the common cases. (default)
2 : Fastest, least faithful. Used by Extreme-2.

When to change: raise it for speed. Drop to 0 if you see jittering geometry, drifting physics, or crackling audio — anything where small numeric errors accumulate.

Which native type Box64 uses to stand in for x87 floating point. x87 works in 80-bit extended precision that ARM has no equivalent for, so something narrower has to be substituted.

0 : Use the narrowest type that fits. Fastest, least precise.
1 : Use double precision throughout. Slower, closer to the original. (default on the safe presets)
2 : Highest precision available. Slowest.

When to change: older games doing serious maths — flight simulators, racing physics, strategy games with large numbers — can drift or desync at 0. Raise it if a game behaves subtly wrong rather than crashing outright.

Dynarec building BigBlock

0 : Don\'t try to build block as big as possible
1 : Build Dynarec block as big as possible
2 : Build Dynarec block bigger (continue when block overlaps, but only for blocks in elf memory)
3 : Build Dynarec block bigger (continue when block overlaps, for all types of memory)

When to change: Higher values give faster sustained frame rates because more of the game loop is optimised together. Lower them if you get a hitch the first time you enter each new area, or if a game generates code as it runs and trips over blocks that span too much memory.

Simulation of Strong Memory model

0 : Don\'t try anything special
1 : Enable some Memory Barrier when writing to memory (on some MOV opcode)
2 : All 1 plus a Memory Barrier on every write to memory using MOV
3 : All 2 plus Memory Barrier when reading from memory and on some SSE/SSE2 opcodes

When to change: Raise it when a multithreaded game crashes at random, corrupts saves, or desyncs in multiplayer — symptoms of writes landing out of order. Lower it for speed once you know a game is happy without it. Unity games generally need at least 1.

How far ahead Box64 will follow a forward jump when deciding how much code to translate into one block.

0 : Stop at the first forward jump. Smallest blocks.
128 / 256 : Modest look-ahead.
512 : Balanced. (default)
1024 : Maximum look-ahead. Biggest, fastest blocks. Used by Extreme-2.

When to change: raise it for more speed in tight game loops. Lower it if you get hitching the first time you enter a new area, since bigger blocks take longer to compile the moment they are first needed.

Optimisation of CALL and RET. Normally every function return is an indirect jump Box64 has to look up; this option keeps a proper return-address stack instead.

0 : Generic handling. Slower, but tolerates programs that play games with return addresses.
1 : Optimised. Noticeably faster in call-heavy code. (default on most presets)

When to change: turn it off for packed, obfuscated or DRM-protected executables that deliberately manipulate the call stack. Crashes deep in unfamiliar code shortly after launch are the usual symptom.

What a thread does when it needs a block another thread is still compiling.

0 : Do not wait — interpret the code in the meantime. No stalls, but that stretch runs slowly.
1 : Wait for the compiled block. Better sustained speed, at the cost of a brief pause. (default)

When to change: set 0 if you get short freezes during loading screens or when first entering an area, especially on a device with fewer cores.

Tweak memory barriers to reduce performance impact of strong memory emulation

0 : Use regular safe barriers
1 : Use weak barriers for mild performance boost
2 : Use weak barriers, additionally disable last write barriers

When to change: A way to keep most of the speed while still emulating strong memory. If a game needs STRONGMEM but the cost is too high, try 1 here first. Drop back to 0 if instability returns — weak barriers fail as random corruption rather than a clean crash.

Generate aligned atomics only (only available on Arm64 for now).

0 : Generate unaligned atomics handling code.
1 : Generate aligned atomics only, which is faster and smaller code size, but will cause SIGBUS for LOCK prefixed opcodes operating on aligned data addresses.

When to change: Leave at 0. Set 1 only for a game you know keeps its atomic data aligned, and be ready to revert: the failure mode is a hard SIGBUS crash the moment a misaligned locked operation is executed.

Deferred flags. x86 updates its condition flags on almost every arithmetic instruction, and the vast majority are never read. Deferring means only working them out when something actually asks.

0 : Compute flags eagerly, every time. Slower, maximally faithful.
1 : Defer until read. Considerably faster. (default)

When to change: almost never — leave it on. Turn it off only when hunting a bug where a game takes visibly wrong decisions: enemies not reacting, doors not opening, checks that should pass and do not.

Allow continue running a block that is unprotected and potentially dirty.

0 : Do not allow continue running a block that is unprotected and potentially dirty.
1 : Allow continue to run a dynablock that write data in the same page as code. It can gets faster in loading time of some game but can also get unexpected crashes.
2 : Will also, when it detect an HotPage, flag that page as NEVERCLEAN, and so it will not be write protected but Block build from that page will always be tested. It can be faster that way (but some SMC case might not be trapped).

When to change: Raise it to speed up loading in games that write data next to their own code. Set it back to 0 if you get unexplained crashes during loading screens or shortly after a level starts.

Whether Box64 uses the ARM chip own condition flags directly instead of keeping emulated x86 flags in memory.

0 : Emulate x86 flags separately. Safe, slower.
1 : Use native ARM flags where the meaning maps exactly. Faster. (used by Extreme-2)

When to change: it is one of the bigger speed levers, so try it on. Set it back to 0 if a game starts behaving illogically — comparisons going the wrong way, AI acting oddly — rather than crashing.

Enable x86 PAUSE emulation, may help the performance of spinlocks.

0 : Ignore x86 PAUSE instruction.
1 : Use YIELD to emulate x86 PAUSE instruction.
2 : Use WFI to emulate x86 PAUSE instruction.
3 : Use SEVL+WFE to emulate x86 PAUSE instruction.

When to change: Matters for games that spin-wait between threads. If a game pegs the CPU and runs hot while doing very little, try 1 or 3 — a proper yield lets the other thread actually make progress instead of both fighting for the core.

AVX and AVX2 implemented, along with BMI1, BMI2, ADX, FMA, F16C and RDANDR extension!

0 : Disable AVX extension
1 : enable AVX, BMI1, F16C and VAES extension.
2 : All 1 plus enable AVX2, BMI2, FMA, ADX,VPCLMULQDQ and RDRAND.
\

When to change: Raise it for modern games that check for AVX or AVX2 and refuse to start without them. Lower it to 0 if a game detects AVX, takes that code path, and then renders incorrectly or crashes — emulated AVX is not always a perfect match.

How many CPU cores Box64 tells the game it has.

0 : Report the real count. (default)
4 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 : Cap the reported count.

When to change: some games create a worker thread per core and fall apart on a many-core phone — stuttering, thread starvation, or a crash at startup. Capping to 4 or 8 often fixes it. A few older titles also break outright above 32.

Detects UnityPlayer.dll and automatically applies the stronger memory ordering Unity games need, without slowing everything else down.

0 : Off. Unity games need STRONGMEM set manually instead.
1 : On. Auto-applied when a Unity game is detected. (default)

When to change: leave it on — it costs nothing for non-Unity games. Turn it off only if you are setting memory ordering by hand and want no surprises.

Forces memory allocations into the low 32-bit address range, so every pointer fits in 32 bits.

0 : Allocate anywhere in the 64-bit space.
1 : Force the low 32-bit space. (default)

When to change: needed by 32-bit games, and by 64-bit games that carelessly store pointers in 32-bit fields. Turn it off for a large 64-bit game that runs out of memory, since the low space is only 4 GB no matter how much RAM the device has.

Total Store Ordering. x86 guarantees that memory writes become visible to other threads in the order they were made; ARM makes no such promise. FEX can enforce it, at a cost.

0 : Off. Clearly faster.
1 : On. Correct for multithreaded games. (default)

When to change: this is the single most important correctness knob. Games that need it and do not get it crash at random, hang, corrupt saves or desync in multiplayer — rarely in the same place twice. Turn it off only for simple or single-threaded games.

Extends store ordering to vector (SIMD) loads and stores, making them atomic as well.

0 : Off. (default on the Performance and Extreme presets)
1 : On. Slower — vector memory traffic is heavy in most games.

When to change: rarely needed. Only games doing multithreaded SIMD work on shared buffers require it. Worth trying if Stability fixes a crash and you are narrowing down which knob was responsible.

Uses cheaper half-barriers for unaligned loads and stores when store ordering is on, instead of full barriers.

0 : Full barriers. Strongest guarantee, slowest.
1 : Half-barriers. Faster, marginally weaker.

When to change: a useful middle ground between Performance and Stability. If a game needs ordering but full barriers cost too much, try turning this on before giving up on speed.

Makes the bulk memory instructions REP MOVS and REP STOS — block copy and block fill — atomic under store ordering.

0 : Off. Faster, and bulk copies are among the hottest operations in a game engine. (default on the fast presets)
1 : On. Slower but correct when threads share the buffers being copied.

When to change: turn it on if a game corrupts textures, audio or save data under load while looking otherwise stable — a sign of one thread reading a buffer another is still copying.

Whether FEX compiles several connected blocks of code together instead of one at a time.

0 : One block at a time. Quick to compile, slower code.
1 : Compile across blocks, so FEX can optimise the whole path. Faster code, longer compiles. (default)

When to change: leave it on for sustained frame rate. Turn it off if first-visit stutter — a hitch the first time you enter each new area, then smooth afterwards — bothers you more than average speed does.

Forces CPU features on or off rather than letting FEX detect them.

off : Detect automatically. (default)
enableavx / disableavx : Force AVX on or off in what the game is told.
enablesve / disablesve : Force the ARM Scalable Vector Extension on or off in what FEX uses internally.

When to change: enableavx for a game that refuses to start claiming it needs AVX; disableavx if a game detects it, takes an AVX code path and then misbehaves. The SVE options are for testing on chips that actually have it.

Scales the CPU timestamp counter, which is what games read to measure elapsed time. Phone counters often tick at a very different rate to the desktop CPUs a game expects.

0 : Pass the counter through unscaled.
1 : Scale it to something the game will interpret sensibly. (default)

When to change: this is the knob for a game running in slow motion or fast-forward, animations playing at the wrong speed, or timers counting wrongly while the frame rate itself looks fine.

64-bit Windows programs can carry volatile metadata: the compiler marking exactly which memory accesses must not be reordered. FEX can read it and apply store ordering only where the game genuinely needs it, rather than everywhere.

0 : Ignore it.
1 : Use it when present. (default)

When to change: leave it on — it is close to free accuracy. It simply has no effect on games built without the metadata.

Workarounds for Mono, the .NET runtime Unity games are built on. Mono generates code while running, which needs special handling around self-modifying-code detection and JIT blocks.

0 : Off.
1 : On. Detects Mono and applies the workarounds. (default)

When to change: leave it on; it only engages for games that need it. Turn it off only to test whether it is implicated in a Unity game misbehaving.

CPUID includes a bit saying whether the code is running under a hypervisor. Emulation looks like a hypervisor, so it is normally set.

0 : Report it honestly.
1 : Hide it, so the game believes it is on bare metal. (default on the Denuvo preset)

When to change: turn it on for a game or anti-cheat that refuses to launch, or exits immediately, because it thinks it is being run in a virtual machine.

FEX keeps translated code in two cache levels. This disables the second, larger one.

0 : Keep the L2 cache. Smoother, uses more memory. (default)
1 : Disable it. Less memory, but code has to be re-translated more often, which shows up as stutter. (used by the Extreme-wn presets)

When to change: turn it on when memory is tight on a large game. Turn it back off if you get recurring hitches in areas you have already visited.

Makes the first-level translated-code cache grow and shrink with demand instead of staying a fixed size.

0 : Fixed size. Predictable, uses its memory whether or not it needs it. (default)
1 : Dynamic. Less memory when idle, occasional stutter as it resizes. (used by the Extreme-wn presets, together with the two heuristic counters below)

When to change: on for memory-constrained devices or very large games; off if you would rather have consistent frame pacing than free memory.

x87 is the old floating-point unit, working in 80-bit extended precision that ARM has no equivalent for.

0 : Emulate the full 80-bit precision. Accurate and slow.
1 : Use ordinary 64-bit doubles instead. Much faster. (default on every preset above Compatibility)

When to change: set it back to 0 if an older game shows rendering bugs, geometry cracks, or physics that slowly drifts wrong over a long session. Modern games rarely use x87 at all, so this costs them nothing either way.
