Player Slots

Decides which XInput player each controller becomes in the game. Player 1 is slot 0, Player 2 is slot 1, and so on.

Auto — the controller takes the next free player in the order pads connect (the normal behaviour).
Player 1–4 — pins that controller to that exact player, every launch.
Ignore — that controller never takes a player slot.

Shared / combined control — assign TWO (or more) devices to the SAME player and they BOTH drive that player at once (for example the on-screen controls plus a physical pad). Their inputs are combined, not fought over.

On-screen controls — the touch pad can be pinned to any player too. A physical pad connected BEFORE launch takes priority in the connect order. The On-screen priority setting decides what happens when a pad connects mid-game: Keep leaves the touch pad where it is, Yield hands Player 1 to the pad and moves the touch pad up, Share makes the pad share the touch pad\'s player.

Reset Input (in-game side menu) rebuilds the controller connection without restarting the game.

Changes made here (out of game) apply on the game\'s next launch; the in-game side menu changes players live. The app-drawer Input Controls copy of this sets the default for newly-created containers.

Auto / Smart — the recommended setting.

Starts at a low delay and only adds more if it actually hears crackling. On DirectAudio that is a 576-frame buffer, about 33 ms total.

The safety net is the point: a fixed low buffer crackles the moment a heavy scene stalls the GPU, while this one grows just enough to stop that and no further.

Pick this unless you have a reason not to.

Low latency — the floor.

One hardware burst: about 25 ms total on DirectAudio, which is as low as anything on Android goes. Adaptive stays on, so a title that cannot hold it grows a step rather than crackling all session.

Measured across three games, one held this comfortably and two needed a step up. Nothing breaks either way — but if you hear anything, Auto is the setting to return to.

Balanced — a calmer buffer that still adapts.

About 47 ms total on DirectAudio (1248 frames). Noticeably later than Auto, and noticeably safer on a device that struggles.

Worth trying if Auto crackles during loading screens or busy scenes.

Stable — biggest safety margin, most delay.

About 83 ms total on DirectAudio (3000 frames). Sound lags visibly behind the picture in fast games, which is the trade you are making.

For weak devices, very demanding games, or anything that crackles on every other setting.

Custom — unlocks the fine-tune rows below.

Every other preset fills those rows in for you and greys them out; they still show what the preset applies, so you can read them before switching.

Only choose this if you want to set the buffer yourself. The "?" on each row explains what it does.

Output mode — which Android audio path is requested.

Low latency asks for the fast path with a high-priority audio thread. On this emulator that is the tested choice: under box64/FEX a normal-priority thread gets preempted by the game and the sound turns choppy.

None is the ordinary path — steadier on paper, choppier here for that reason.

Power saving favours battery over delay.

DirectAudio forces Low latency for every named preset regardless of this row; it only takes effect on Custom.

Adaptive buffer — grow only when something actually goes wrong.

The buffer starts small. Each time the audio underruns, a little is added, so it settles at the lowest delay this game can hold on your device rather than a number someone guessed.

Turning it off pins the buffer. If the game then cannot keep up, it crackles until you relaunch — nothing recovers on its own.

Every preset now leaves this on, so switching it off is a deliberate choice you make here, on Custom. Do that only when you are testing a fixed size and want no interference.

Audio buffer — how much sound DirectAudio keeps ready, in milliseconds.

Smaller is tighter but more fragile; larger rides out stutters at the cost of delay.

The row shows the total, because Android adds a fixed 21 ms of its own that no application can avoid. A 12 ms buffer is 33 ms total. The lowest possible is one hardware burst — 4 ms of buffer, 25 ms total, the floor for any app on this device.

With adaptive on, this is a starting point and the level the buffer returns to once things are calm again — it never drops below what you set here.

Guest buffer — how much sound Windows hands to PulseAudio at a time.

This is the guest side of the delay, separate from the sink buffer below. It is fixed when the game connects, so a change takes effect on the next launch.

Lower means tighter sync and more work per second; higher is steadier.

Initial buffer — the starting size, in audio frames rather than milliseconds.

48 frames is 1 ms, so 576 frames is a 12 ms buffer (33 ms total). auto lets the engine choose.

This is the advanced form of the millisecond row above. If you set both, frames win — clear it back to auto to go by milliseconds again.

Max buffer — how far adaptive growth is allowed to go.

A ceiling, not a target: the buffer only reaches it if the game repeatedly underruns. It stops a bad patch from inflating the delay without limit.

device max uses the driver default (100 ms). Setting it too low means a struggling game runs out of room and keeps crackling.

Not used by ALSA.

This row sets the guest-side buffer, which only PulseAudio has. ALSA reaches Android through the app\'s own sound server, and that takes its sizing from the Initial buffer and Max buffer rows below instead.

Change those to adjust ALSA\'s delay. This slider is greyed out here because nothing reads it.

Turning this on records raw in-game frames while you play, to help train an open, clean frame-generation model. Please read this before enabling.

WHAT IS CAPTURED
• Only the game's raw rendered frames, straight from the game, while you play.

WHAT IS NOT CAPTURED
• NO personal information of any kind.
• NO account, login, name, or email.
• NO Android system data.
• NO audio.
• NO full-screen or system video — nothing outside the game's rendered image, and no HUD or overlay.

ANONYMOUS BY DESIGN
• Each capture file carries a small consent record that is anonymous: only a random anonymous ID, the terms version, a timestamp, and the app version (and optionally your device model, for dataset-diversity stats only). It cannot identify you.

WHERE IT IS SAVED
• Files are written to the Download/win-fg folder on this device, for you to share with us.

GOOD TO KNOW
• Recording lowers your FPS while it runs.
• You can turn this off at any time from Settings.

By ticking "I understand" below you agree that the captured game frames may be used to train the model, and you confirm this is willingly created and shared.

Whether the driver shrinks its buffer back down after a quiet spell, recovering latency it took to survive a rough patch.

0 : Stay at the grown size.
1 : Shrink back when things settle.

When to change: leave it on — it is what stops one bad moment costing you latency for the whole session. Turn it off if audio repeatedly grows and shrinks in a way you can hear.

A ceiling on how far the driver backs off after repeated dropouts.

When to change: raise it for a device that struggles persistently, so the driver is allowed to settle somewhere genuinely safe. Lower it to keep latency bounded.

How long the driver holds off shrinking after a dropout.

When to change: raise it if the buffer shrinks too eagerly and dropouts return. This is the brake on the decay behaviour.

How long the audio path must run cleanly before the driver considers shrinking the buffer.

When to change: raise it to make shrinking more cautious, which suits a device that has occasional bursts of load. Lower it to recover latency sooner after a rough patch.

Asks Android for exclusive access to the audio device, bypassing the normal mixer.

0 : Shared.
1 : Exclusive — lower latency where the device allows it.

When to change: turn it on to chase the lowest audio delay. Not every device grants it, and where it is granted other apps may be unable to play sound at the same time.

Logging for the DirectAudio driver.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: turn it on when reporting an audio problem, so the buffer sizes and dropout counts are recorded. Turn it back off afterwards.

The largest buffer the adaptive path may grow to, in milliseconds.

When to change: DirectAudio grows its buffer when it detects dropouts. This caps how far. Raise it for a device that keeps crackling under load; lower it to keep latency bounded even if that means occasional dropouts.

A floor on the wake-up interval, so the driver cannot spin too fast.

When to change: raise it if audio is costing noticeable CPU or battery. Too high and the driver cannot refill the buffer in time.

Target audio buffer size in milliseconds for our DirectAudio driver.

Smaller means less delay between action and sound, and more risk of crackling. Larger is safer.

When to change: the audio settings dialog sets this for you from a preset — only touch it in Custom mode. Raise it if audio crackles, lower it if sound lags the action. Values above about 62.5 ms leave the range we have tested as safe.

How often the audio driver wakes to hand over more samples.

When to change: shorter periods mean tighter timing and more CPU wake-ups. Leave it alone unless you are tuning against a specific dropout pattern.

How long the audio path must be silent before the watchdog treats it as stalled.

When to change: lower it to recover from stalls faster, at the risk of restarting audio during a legitimately quiet passage. Raise it if you hear audio restarting when nothing was wrong.

Watches for the audio path stalling and restarts it.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: leave it on. Without it, an audio stall is permanent for that session — sound simply stops and does not come back.

Forces every block to use two partitions rather than choosing per block.

0 : Choose per block.
1 : Always two.

When to change: mostly a quality experiment. It costs time on blocks that gain nothing from it, so it is usually worse value than BCN_ASTC_TRY_2P alone.

Lets the ASTC encoder try two-partition blocks, which represent detailed areas better.

0 : Single partition only. Faster.
1 : Try two. Higher quality, slower.

When to change: turn it on if transcoded textures look blocky. Expect longer loading.

Makes the ASTC encoder search in coarser steps.

0 : Fine search. Slower, better quality.
1 : Coarse search. Faster, lower quality.

When to change: from the Fcharan fork of the BCn layer. Turn it on when loading times matter more than texture quality.

Lets the compute layer decide for itself whether transcoding is needed.

0 : Follow the explicit settings.
1 : Auto-detect.

When to change: auto is the sensible default. Turn it off when you want to force a specific target format regardless of what the layer would choose.

Uses the storage-image path for compute transcoding rather than the buffer path.

0 : Buffer path.
1 : Storage image path.

When to change: an alternative implementation — try the other setting if textures come out corrupted or the layer crashes.

How much the BCn layer logs, for example info or error.

When to change: raise it while diagnosing texture problems, then set it back. Texture transcoding happens constantly, so verbose logging here is expensive.

Memory budget for textures waiting to be transcoded, in megabytes.

When to change: raise it if loading is slow and the device has memory to spare — more staging room means fewer stalls. Lower it if a game runs out of memory during loading.

Logs timing for every texture transfer the layer handles.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: diagnosis only — for working out whether transcoding is what is making loading slow. It is noisy and costs performance itself.

How many transcode jobs may be queued at once.

When to change: lower it if transcoding starves the game of GPU time and the frame rate dips during loading. Raise it to prioritise getting textures ready sooner.

Target ASTC when re-encoding BCn textures. ASTC is the format Mali GPUs handle best.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: the usual choice on Mali. Needs the compute layer enabled. Higher quality than ETC but slower to produce.

Target ETC1, the oldest and most widely supported compressed format.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: a last resort. ETC1 has no alpha channel, so transparency suffers — use ETC2 or ASTC where possible.

Target ETC2 instead of ASTC. ETC2 is supported on essentially every Android GPU.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: when ASTC is unavailable or too slow. Quality is lower than ASTC, particularly on textures with sharp detail or alpha.

Emulates null descriptors, letting shaders reference resources that are not bound.

0 : Off.
1 : Emulate.

When to change: a DX12 requirement on the compat layer. Without it, games that leave slots unbound crash on the first draw call that touches one.

Emulates push descriptors, a fast way of handing shader parameters to the GPU.

0 : Off.
1 : Emulate.

When to change: leave it on for DX12 titles on the compat layer — several use push descriptors and will not start without it.

Emulates sparse binding — the ability to build a large resource from scattered pieces of memory — which Mali does not support.

0 : Off.
1 : Emulate.

When to change: needed by games using tiled or streaming resources, which otherwise fail at startup. Emulation costs memory and speed, so leave it off for games that do not need it.

Forces the compat layer to apply write masking rather than relying on the driver.

0 : Off.
1 : Force.

When to change: a rendering-correctness workaround. Try it when colours or transparency come out wrong on Mali in a way no other setting explains.

Compiles shader pipelines in the background instead of stopping the game to wait.

0 : Off. Correct but stuttery on first encounter with new effects.
1 : On. Far smoother, at the cost of objects briefly rendering wrong or not at all while their shader compiles.

When to change: turn it on for stutter-prone games. Only works on DXVK builds with async support — ours are gplasync builds, which have it.

DXVK settings written inline, as key=value pairs separated by semicolons.

When to change: for one-off tweaks without maintaining a file — for example d3d11.maxFeatureLevel=11_0 to force an older feature level for a game that misdetects. DXVK_CONFIG_FILE is easier for anything longer.

Path to a dxvk.conf file holding DXVK settings.

When to change: when you have a set of tweaks to reuse, or a per-game config someone else published. The path is inside the container, so it is usually somewhere under the game folder or the Windows drive.

Makes DXVK avoid Vulkan timeline semaphores and use the older synchronisation path.

0 : Use them. (default)
1 : Avoid them.

When to change: a compatibility fallback for drivers whose timeline semaphore support is buggy — the symptom is a hang or a GPU crash rather than anything visual.

Restricts DXVK to a GPU whose name contains this text.

When to change: only useful on a device exposing more than one Vulkan GPU, where DXVK chooses the wrong one. Leave it blank otherwise — a name that matches nothing leaves the game with no GPU at all.

Caps the frame rate inside DXVK itself.

0 : No cap.
Any other number: that many frames per second.

When to change: capping to 30 or 60 on a phone often gives smoother, cooler, longer-lasting play than letting a game run flat out. Also useful for games whose physics or timers misbehave at very high frame rates.

Caches the results of async pipeline compilation between runs.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: pairs with DXVK_ASYNC — turning both on means the brief visual glitches while shaders compile happen once rather than every session.

DXVK’s on-screen overlay. Pick any combination of items.

fps frame rate · frametimes a frame-time graph · gpuload GPU utilisation · memory video memory · devinfo GPU name and driver · drawcalls, pipelines, compiler workload detail · scale= and opacity= control appearance.

When to change: add fps plus gpuload when you want to know whether a game is limited by the GPU or something else. compiler is useful when diagnosing stutter, since it shows shader compilation happening. Turn it all off for normal play — the overlay itself costs a little.

How much DXVK writes to its log file.

none · error · warn · info · debug, in increasing detail.

When to change: raise it to info or debug when diagnosing a graphics problem — the log records the GPU, driver, extensions and DXVK version, which is usually the first thing worth checking. Put it back afterwards; debug logging is slow.

Whether DXVK saves compiled shader pipelines to disk so later runs start warm.

0 : Off, recompile every run.
1 : On. (default)

When to change: leave it on — the first playthrough of an area stutters while shaders compile, and the cache is what stops that happening again. Turn it off only if a corrupt cache is causing crashes, then delete the cache file.

Switches on the standalone BCn compute layer, which ships separately from the driver wrapper.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: this is the important one on Mali with the Original wrapper, which has no BCn support of its own — the compute layer is then the only way compressed textures work at all. Pair it with WRAPPER_EMULATE_BCN=0 so the work is not done twice. Unnecessary on Adreno.

Enables the compatibility layer that fills in D3D features Mali GPUs lack.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: Mali devices only, and required for many DX11 and DX12 games there. It does nothing on Adreno.

Whether FEX saves the x86 code it has translated to disk so later runs start warm. Translation normally happens fresh every launch and is thrown away when the game closes.

0 : Off, translate everything again each run. (default)
1 : On, reuse what was translated before.

When to change: turn it on for a game that stutters as new areas load, or one with a long first-time load. The gain shows on the second and later launches, once the cache has something in it. Needs FEXCore 2609 or newer; older builds ignore the variable.

Risk: upstream has not added any cleanup yet, so the cache has no size limit and never drops old entries — it only grows, and grows fastest on games that generate their own code as they run. It may also miss that a game has been updated and keep stale entries. The cache lives in the container AppData folder; delete it if space runs short or a game misbehaves after an update.

Overrides device feature flags in the freedreno/Turnip driver.

enable_tp_ubwc_flag_hint=1 and storage_8bit=1 switch on capabilities the driver otherwise leaves off.

When to change: only when a specific guide for a specific game tells you to. These change what the driver claims to support, and getting it wrong produces corruption rather than a clean error.

A performance overlay drawn by Mesa’s Gallium drivers, separate from the DXVK one.

simple · fps · frametime.

When to change: only useful for OpenGL games, since DXVK titles will not show it. For D3D games use DXVK_HUD instead.

Flags for the Adreno shader compiler inside Mesa.

nouboopt, nopreamble, noearlypreamble each disable a compiler optimisation.

When to change: only to work around a shader compiler bug producing corrupted graphics in a specific game. Each one costs performance.

Hides any OpenGL extension introduced after the given year.

When to change: for old games that walk the extension list and break on anything they do not recognise. Setting something like 2005 makes the driver look like hardware of that era.

Forces the OpenGL version string reported to the game, for example 4.6 or 3.3COMPAT.

When to change: for an OpenGL game that refuses to start because it thinks the driver is too old. Claiming a version the driver cannot actually deliver usually ends in a crash instead, so it is a gamble either way.

Runs OpenGL command submission on its own thread.

false : Off.
true : On — can help when the game’s main thread is the bottleneck.

When to change: worth trying for OpenGL games that are CPU-limited. It can also cause stutter or crashes in games that use GL from several threads themselves.

Skips OpenGL error checking for a small speed gain.

0 : Normal checking. (default)
1 : Skip it.

When to change: rarely worth it. A game that generates errors will misbehave unpredictably rather than fail cleanly, which makes any other problem much harder to diagnose.

Turns off Mesa’s on-disk shader cache.

false : Cache enabled. (default)
true : Disabled — recompile every run.

When to change: essentially never, except to test whether a corrupt cache is causing crashes or artefacts. Leaving it disabled means permanent first-run stutter.

How finished frames are handed to the display.

fifo : Wait for the display. No tearing, capped to the refresh rate. Most power-efficient.
mailbox : Keep the newest frame ready, discard older ones. Smooth and tear-free, uses more power.
immediate : Show frames as soon as they are done. Lowest lag, can tear.
relaxed : Like fifo but allows tearing when the game falls behind.

When to change: frame generation needs mailbox or immediate — it does nothing on fifo. Otherwise fifo is the sane default, and immediate is for chasing minimum input lag.

How much audio PulseAudio buffers ahead, in milliseconds.

Lower means more responsive sound and a higher risk of crackling. Higher means safer but more delayed audio.

When to change: raise it (60-120) if audio crackles or drops out under load. Lower it (20-40) if sound noticeably lags the action. Only applies to the PulseAudio backend.

Debug and behaviour flags for Turnip, the open-source Vulkan driver for Adreno GPUs.

Most are diagnostic (startup, perf, nir), while others disable optimisations (noubwc, nolrz, sysmem, forcebin).

When to change: the disable flags are compatibility workarounds — nolrz and noubwc in particular fix rendering glitches on some games at a cost in speed. The diagnostic flags belong in a bug report, not in normal play.

VKD3D behaviour flags, several allowed at once.

When to change: these are targeted workarounds — most are for specific bugs in specific games. Leave it empty unless a per-game guide tells you otherwise.

How much VKD3D writes to its log.

none · err · fixme · warn · trace, in increasing detail.

When to change: raise it when a D3D12 game misbehaves. trace is enormous and slow — use it only briefly.

The highest D3D12 feature level VKD3D reports.

12_2 down to 11_0.

When to change: lower it for a game that asks for features the GPU lacks and crashes rather than falling back. Raise it only if a game refuses to start claiming the hardware is too old.

The highest D3D12 shader model VKD3D reports to the game.

6_6 down to 5_1, newest first.

When to change: lower it when a game requests shaders your driver cannot actually compile — the symptom is a crash or black rendering shortly after loading. Lowering it makes the game pick a simpler path.

How many frames VKD3D lets the game queue ahead of the display.

Lower means less input lag but more chance of the GPU idling. Higher means smoother pacing and more lag.

When to change: lower it (1 or 2) if a D3D12 game feels laggy to control. Raise it if the frame rate is uneven despite the GPU having headroom.

Wine normally intercepts a game’s fullscreen resolution change and fakes it, so the desktop stays at its real resolution.

0 : Keep the hack. (default)
1 : Disable it and let the game change the mode for real.

When to change: disable it if a game’s fullscreen is stretched, offset, or shows the wrong part of the screen.

Stops Wine creating the DXGI device manager that hardware video decoding hangs off.

0 : Normal behaviour.
1 : Skip it.

When to change: a workaround for games that crash or hang on startup while setting up video playback — typically at an intro movie or a cutscene.

Our own fast-yield gate. Some games spin a worker thread that repeatedly asks the system to let something else run; on a phone that ends up pegging one core at 100% regardless of your frame cap.

0 : Normal yield behaviour. (default)
1 : Make the yield a no-op so the thread stops burning the core.

When to change: turn it on for a game where one core sits at 100% and the device runs hot while the frame rate is capped and fine. Tester-measured on Cyberpunk: prime core 100% down to roughly 0-3%, power ~5.3W down to ~3.9W, frame rate unchanged.

Risk: a no-op yield can starve the thread that was waiting to run, which hangs some games. It also needs a layer built with the gate — Proton 10.0-2 and newer have it; older layers ignore the variable entirely.

AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution upscaling for fullscreen games. Renders at a lower internal resolution and upscales, which can be a large speed win.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: turn it on when a game runs slowly at native resolution. It only applies to games running genuinely fullscreen at a lower-than-native resolution — a game already at native resolution has nothing to upscale.

How aggressively FSR sharpens the upscaled image. Lower is sharper.

Typical range 0 to 5; 2 is a common middle ground.

When to change: only meaningful with WINE_FULLSCREEN_FSR on. Lower it if the image looks soft, raise it if sharpening makes edges look harsh or noisy.

Stops GStreamer, which decodes in-game video, from using the GPU.

0 : Allow GPU decoding.
1 : Force CPU decoding.

When to change: set it to 1 if cutscenes crash, freeze the game, or show corrupted video. CPU decoding is slower but far more reliable under emulation.

Selects Wine’s newer media pipeline for in-game video.

0 : Old pipeline.
1 : New pipeline.

When to change: try the other setting when cutscenes are black, silent, stuttering or hang the game. Which one works varies by title.

Mesa\'s OpenGL vsync control.

0 : Never wait for the screen refresh (vsync off).

When to change: use Vsync off in the OpenGL card in the container or game settings instead; it sets vblank_mode=0. A value typed here is kept and wins over the switch.

Overrides the Fast OpenGL setting.

1 : On through Wine\'s EGL backend, even where the setting is off or greyed (still needs the libraries bundled with the app, and a layer whose Wine has the EGL backend).
0 : Off, whatever the setting says (also beats WINHUB_X11_GLX).

When to change: almost never — use Fast in the OpenGL card in the container or game settings, which picks EGL or GLX by layer. This is for testing a layer or driver the switch does not offer it on.

Forces Fast OpenGL through GLX: the X server turns on its own GLX support (and DRI3/Present 1.2) for the session, and Wine\'s GLX loads the bundled OpenGL library with Zink.

1 : GLX route on, whatever the layer.

When to change: to try the GLX route on a layer that would otherwise use EGL. Older Wine and x86-64 layers already take this route. WINHUB_X11_EGL=0 still turns Fast OpenGL off.

Forces the X11 driver down the GLX path rather than its newer default.

0 : Normal.
1 : Force GLX.

When to change: a compatibility fallback for OpenGL games that render black or fail to create a context.

Wine’s logging channels. Controls what goes into wine_debug.log.

-all : Silence everything. Fastest.
fixme-all : Hide the noisy fixme messages, keep errors.
+seh : Exception detail — useful for crashes.
+relay : Every API call. Enormous and very slow.
warn+all : Everything at warning level and above.

When to change: leave it alone unless you are diagnosing something. Custom values like "+loaddll,+seh" are kept as typed. Logging costs real performance, and a hang with logging on can write hundreds of megabytes.

Tells Wine whether to use its own version of a DLL or one shipped with the game.

Format is name=b for Wine’s builtin, name=n for the game’s native file, or name=n,b to prefer native and fall back. Several are separated by semicolons.

When to change: the usual case is a game shipping its own copy of a library that works better than Wine’s, or the reverse. The editor detects DLLs in the game folder and offers a toggle per file, which is easier than typing this by hand.

Eventfd-based thread synchronisation. Windows programs wait on each other constantly; esync makes those waits far cheaper than Wine’s default server round-trip.

0 : Off, use the normal Wine server path.
1 : On. Often a large frame-rate gain in threaded games.

When to change: on by default in most of our layers and usually worth having. Turn it off if a game deadlocks or hangs on a loading screen — esync is known to deadlock some titles.

Futex-based synchronisation. Same purpose as esync but using a newer kernel mechanism, generally faster where the kernel supports it.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: needs kernel support that many Android devices lack, and it is silently ignored where unavailable. If enabling it changes nothing, your kernel does not have it — esync is the fallback.

Caps the video memory Wine reports to the game, in megabytes.

When to change: some games misbehave when told the GPU has an unusual amount of memory — allocating far too much and running out, or refusing to start. Setting a sane figure such as 2048 or 4096 can fix that. Leave it unset unless a game has a memory-related problem.

Re-encodes BCn textures to ASTC, which Mali GPUs do read natively. Part of the wrapper’s integrated path.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: for Mali devices running games with compressed textures, when using a wrapper that carries the integrated path. This path is ASTC only — ETC needs the standalone layer.

Does the BCn decode work on the GPU rather than the CPU.

0 : CPU.
1 : GPU.

When to change: GPU decode is usually much faster and cuts loading times, but uses GPU time the game also wants. Switch back to CPU if enabling it costs frame rate.

Reports a different Vulkan device ID to the game.

When to change: paired with the vendor ID for games that identify the GPU by number and take a hardware-specific path. Rarely needed.

Reports a different GPU name to the game.

When to change: for games that check the GPU name and refuse to run, or enable a broken vendor-specific path. Purely cosmetic to the driver — it changes only what the game is told.

Turns on the wrapper’s own diagnostic logging.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: for diagnosing driver-level problems, and worth turning off afterwards — logging on the graphics path costs performance.

Disables placed memory allocations in the wrapper.

0 : Normal.
1 : Disabled.

When to change: a compatibility toggle for drivers that mishandle this allocation style. Try it for memory-related crashes that no other setting fixes.

Stops the wrapper using the present-wait extension for frame pacing.

0 : Use it.
1 : Disable it.

When to change: a fallback for drivers whose present-wait is broken. The symptom is the game hanging at the point it tries to show its first frame.

Overrides the driver identity string the wrapper reports.

When to change: some games and layers take a different code path per driver vendor. Changing this can dodge a driver-specific workaround that is doing more harm than good on our stack.

BCn texture emulation inside the driver wrapper. Desktop games ship BC/DXT compressed textures that Mali GPUs cannot read natively.

0 : Off.
1 : Basic.
2 : Full.
3 : Auto. (default)

When to change: only the leegao and GameNative wrappers implement this — the Winlator base and Bionic wrappers ignore it. On Adreno it is unnecessary, since those GPUs read BCn natively. Set it to 0 if you are using the standalone compute layer instead, to avoid transcoding twice.

A comma-separated list of Vulkan extensions to hide from the game.

When to change: when a game uses an extension the driver reports but does not implement well — the result is usually corruption or a GPU hang. Hiding it forces the game down a working path.

Caps how many images the swapchain may hold.

Fewer images means less lag and less memory; more means smoother pacing.

When to change: setting 2 or 3 can reduce input lag. Too few can make the frame rate uneven, since the GPU waits for an image to become free.

Transcodes textures on the thread that needs them instead of on a background worker.

0 : Background thread. (default)
1 : Inline.

When to change: a debugging and stability fallback. Inline transcoding stalls the game while it happens, so expect longer loading pauses.

Stops the wrapper rewriting a particular SPIR-V shader construct before handing it to the driver.

0 : Patch as usual. (default)
1 : Leave shaders alone.

When to change: the patch exists to work around driver bugs; disabling it is worth trying if shaders fail to compile or render incorrectly on a driver that does not need the workaround.

Uses a simpler depth buffer format than the game asked for.

0 : Honour the request.
1 : Reduce it.

When to change: compatibility for GPUs that struggle with certain depth formats. Symptoms are z-fighting, missing geometry, or shadows rendering wrong.

Overrides how the wrapper classifies graphics resources.

When to change: an advanced compatibility knob — leave it blank unless a per-game guide specifies a value.

Creates the Vulkan device more conservatively, requesting fewer optional features at once.

0 : Normal.
1 : Safe path.

When to change: try it when a game crashes immediately at startup, before anything renders — that pattern often means device creation failed.

Caches transcoded textures so the work happens once rather than every time a texture loads.

0 : Off.
1 : On.

When to change: worth having on if you have the storage — it noticeably cuts repeat loading times. Turn it off if space is tight.

Reports a different GPU vendor ID to the game.

When to change: for games that enable vendor-specific rendering paths. Claiming a vendor whose extensions the driver lacks usually makes things worse, so change it only on advice.

The Vulkan version the wrapper reports to the game, for example 1.4.

When to change: for a game or translation layer that refuses to run against the version the driver actually reports. Claiming a version the driver cannot deliver moves the failure later rather than fixing it.

Caps the video memory the wrapper reports, in megabytes. 0 leaves it unset.

When to change: for games that allocate based on reported memory and then run out, or that refuse to start when the figure looks wrong. A round number like 2048 or 4096 is a reasonable starting point.

Debug flags for the Zink OpenGL-on-Vulkan layer.

validation enables the Vulkan validation layers; sync forces synchronous submission; nir, spirv and tgsi dump shader stages.

When to change: diagnosis only. sync is occasionally useful to establish whether a crash is a synchronisation problem, but everything here is slow.

How Zink — which runs OpenGL on top of Vulkan — manages descriptors.

auto : Let Zink decide. (default)
lazy : Simplest and often fastest.
cached : Reuse descriptor sets.
notemplates : Avoid update templates, a compatibility fallback.

When to change: only applies to OpenGL games running through Zink. lazy is worth trying for speed, notemplates if you get driver crashes.

Name

The label this entry shows on its card in your library. It reaches neither the Steam client nor the games the client launches - it is only how you find this entry in the app.

Icon

The picture this entry shows on its card in your library. It reaches neither the Steam client nor the games the client launches - it is only artwork for the app.

Screen Size

The resolution the Linux session renders at. It sets the size of gamescope\'s output, so it reaches both the Steam client and every game the client launches - Big Picture and the games inside it all draw into that one output. A smaller size is less work for the GPU and is scaled up to fill your screen.

Screen Alignment

Where the session\'s picture sits on your screen when it does not fill it - centred, at the top, or at the bottom. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches, because they share one output. Top or bottom frees the other half of the screen for on-screen controls.

Fullscreen Mode

How the session\'s picture is fitted to your screen when the two shapes do not match - left alone, fitted with black bars, stretched, filled, or scaled in whole steps. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches, since both render into the same output.

HDR Output

Sends the session\'s picture to your screen in HDR. The compositor opens the HDR path for the whole session, so it reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches. On a screen that does not report HDR10 the setting is greyed out and the session runs in ordinary SDR.

Prefer game-folder DLLs

Makes a game load its own copies of certain support DLLs instead of the ones Proton ships, which is what many wrappers and mod loaders need. This is for the games the client launches only - the Steam client is a native Linux program and has no Windows DLLs. The session has one environment for everything in it, so this applies to every game you start from the client, not to one game.

Environment Variables

Extra settings handed to the Linux session when it starts. They reach both the Steam client and the games the client launches: the client is started with them, and every game inherits them through Steam and Proton. A variable set here overrides the same name coming from the FEXCore preset.

Frame Rate Limiter

Not used by the Steam client. The compositor\'s rate is set once for the whole session, so a cap meant for a game would also hold the client\'s menus to it - a limiter at 60 ran Big Picture at 60 on a 144 Hz screen. A Linux session always runs at this screen\'s highest refresh rate instead. To cap a particular game, use that game\'s own settings.

FEXCore Preset

Tunes FEX, which translates a game\'s x86 code to ARM. It is for the games the client launches only: those run x86 code inside Proton, while the Steam client is a native ARM64 build and never goes through FEX. The preset is handed to the session at launch, and anything you set in Environment Variables overrides it.

Controls Profile

Which on-screen control layout the session uses. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches: the overlay sits over the whole session, so the same buttons drive Big Picture and the game inside it. Left on None, the session brings up the bundled Virtual Gamepad layout when no physical controller is connected.

Touchscreen Mode

Makes a touch act as a tap at the place you touched instead of moving a mouse pointer there. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches, because it changes how the whole session receives your touches.

Hide on-screen controls when a controller connects

Takes the on-screen buttons away as soon as a physical controller is connected, and brings them back when it goes. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches, because the overlay covers the whole session.

Player Slots

Pins your controllers to player 1, 2, 3 and 4 so they stop swapping places between launches. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches, because the session hands the pads on in the order set here. Leave it on the container default unless a pad keeps arriving as the wrong player.

Motion Aim

Turns tilting the device into aiming or pointer movement. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches, because the motion is fed in as controller or mouse input for the whole session. The finer numbers - deadzone and smoothing - live in Container Settings.

Processor Affinity

Chooses which CPU cores the session is allowed to run on. It reaches both the Steam client and the games the client launches: the compositor finds each program by its real process id and pins it to these cores. Leaving every core ticked lets Android place the work itself, which is usually the best choice.

Steam client cores

Chooses which CPU cores the Steam client and the compositor drawing its interface may run on. It reaches the client and its menus only, never the games it launches - those have their own list below. Steam holds its own interface renderer to a subset of this device\'s cores by default, which is why Big Picture can feel sluggish; what you tick here replaces that choice.

Game cores

Chooses which CPU cores a game launched from the Steam client may run on. It reaches games only - the client and its menus keep the list above. Leaving every core ticked lets Android place the work itself, which is usually the best choice.

"Draw driver (Linux runtime) — Linux Steam client only.

This is the Vulkan driver that draws inside the Linux runtime. Everything in the session uses it: gamescope's compositing, the Steam client's own interface (its OpenGL goes through the runtime's Zink to Vulkan) and every game the client launches (Direct3D goes through Proton's DXVK/VKD3D to Vulkan). One choice covers the client and its games.

Runtime default is the Turnip the runtime was built with. Anything else is a driver you imported under Contents → Installed → Linux runtime drivers. Only -Linux Turnip zips can be imported: the client and its games are Linux processes and cannot load an Android or Wayland driver at all.

Nothing inside the runtime is modified — the Vulkan loader is simply pointed at the driver you picked, so switching back is instant. If an imported driver is deleted, the session quietly uses the runtime default again.

This is not the driver that puts the picture on the screen. That is Display driver (Android side) above, and both are always involved: this one draws the frame, that one shows it."

Display driver (Android side)

Two graphics drivers are involved in a Linux session and this is one of them. This is the Android driver the app loads to take the session\'s finished frames and put them on your screen. It affects both the Steam client and its games, because everything you see goes through it. Setting it to System gives a black screen. What the client and its games actually render with is a separate driver inside the Linux runtime, which is not chosen here.

Audio Driver

How sound leaves the session and reaches Android. On this path only PulseAudio carries sound, and it carries it for both the Steam client and the games the client launches. Every other value leaves the whole session silent, so keep this on PulseAudio.

Microphone

Lets a game use the microphone for voice chat. It is meant for the games the client launches, not for the Steam client. It does nothing in a Linux session yet: the switch is wired for the Windows side, and the Linux side that would carry the sound in is not in place.

Mali (PanVK)

For FristOneRR\'s PanVK driver on an Arm Mali GPU (github.com/FristOneRR/FristOneRR-Panvk-Driver, MIT licence). Mali mode applies FristOneRR\'s tweaks in the Wayland adapter: it hides VK_KHR_present_id, VK_KHR_present_wait and VK_KHR_dynamic_rendering from the game, and turns on its two sync workarounds for this driver (skip GPU submit waits, skip the frame-acquire signal). Each of the three has its own switch under Advanced; the two sync workarounds are for DXVK games, so turn them off if a D3D12 game misbehaves or you see tearing. It turns on by itself when the driver\'s name contains \'panvk\'; you can switch it either way.

BCn textures
Turning Mali mode on sets BCn texture emulation to none. Converting BCn textures to ASTC can freeze or reboot the phone with this driver; only try another setting if a game shows broken or missing textures.

Advanced
The driver variables FristOneRR lists as safe. Left on Auto / Default they are not set at all. PANVK_ATOM_STRIDE is only for when auto-detection fails ([KFAULT] in the log); PANVK_TRACE adds driver tracing to the log.
